It peaks on the operative word of the notice (copyright, rights, license, warranty, reproduce, redistribute, cookies, subscribe, unsubscribe) but stays at its floor when those words appear in ordinary descriptive prose (a car warranty, a driver's licence, human rights) or in legal boilerplate about other matters (safety warnings, sale terms), with the exception that the bare word 'cookies' carries direct lexical weight even outside a consent notice.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Each autumn, millions of songbirds leave their breeding grounds in the northern forests and follow ancient migration routes south. Researchers have tracked these journeys for decades with leg bands, radar, and tiny geolocators that weigh less than a paper clip. The data reveal remarkable feats of endurance. A single blackpoll warbler can fly more than two thousand kilometres over open ocean without stopping to rest or feed, and the ruby-throated hummingbird, which weighs about as much as a penny, crosses the Gulf of Mexico in one nonstop flight before refuelling on nectar for days. Scientists are still working out how the birds navigate. Some cues are obvious, such as the position of the sun and the patterns of the stars, but others remain mysterious. Experiments in planetariums have shown that many species orient themselves by the Earth's magnetic field, sensing it through specialised cells in their eyes. Weather shapes the timing of migration as well. A cold front sweeping down from Canada can push thousands of birds south in a single night, while warm southerly winds may persuade them to linger a little longer. Cities present new hazards. Artificial light disorients night migrants and draws them toward tall buildings, and glass windows reflect the sky in ways that birds cannot interpret. Conservation groups now promote lights-out campaigns during the peak weeks of migration, and some cities have changed their building codes in response. Volunteers walk the streets before dawn, collecting stunned birds that have struck windows and releasing them in safer places. The work is slow and often heartbreaking, but the volunteers keep detailed records, and those records have helped identify the buildings that cause the most collisions. Climate change is shifting the calendar too: spring arrives earlier in many regions, and some species now nest weeks sooner than they did fifty years ago.
